content: RalA, also known as Ras-related protein Ral-A, is a protein encoded by the RALA gene located on chromosome 7 in humans. It is one of two paralogs of the Ral protein family, the other being RalB, and is a member of the Ras GTPase family. RalA functions as a molecular switch, playing a critical role in activating various biological processes, particularly those related to cell division and intracellular transport, through its involvement in signaling pathways. Due to its biological functions, RalA has been implicated in the progression of several cancers. Structure RalA and RalB share approximately 80% similarity in their overall amino acid sequences and exhibit 100% identity in their effector-binding regions. However, the two isoforms differ significantly in their C-terminal hypervariable regions, which contain multiple sites for post-translational modifications. These modifications result in distinct subcellular localizations and biological functions. For instance, phosphorylation of serine 194 on RalA by the kinase Aurora A leads to its relocation to the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it facilitates mitochondrial fission. In contrast, phosphorylation of serine 198 on RalB by protein kinase C (PKC) directs RalB to other internal membranes, where it activates its tumorigenic functions. Function RalA is one of the two proteins in the Ral family, which is a subfamily within the Ras family of small GTPases. As a Ras GTPase, RalA operates as a molecular switch, becoming active when bound to GTP and inactive when bound to GDP. RalA can be activated by Ral guanine nucleotide exchange factors (RalGEFs) and, in turn, activates downstream effectors in signal transduction pathways, leading to specific biological outcomes. For example, RalA interacts with components of the exocyst complex, such as Exo84 and Sec5, to promote autophagosome assembly, secretory vesicle trafficking, and tethering. Other downstream functions of RalA include exocytosis, receptor-mediated endocytosis, tight junction biogenesis, filopodia formation, mitochondrial fission, and cytokinesis. Ral-mediated exocytosis is involved in various biological processes, including platelet activation, immune cell functions, neuronal plasticity, and the regulation of insulin action. While many of these functions are shared between RalA and RalB, their distinct subcellular localizations result in differential involvement in specific biological processes. Notably, RalA is more prominently involved in anchorage-independent cell growth, vesicle trafficking, and cytoskeletal organization. Additionally, RalA specifically interacts with Exo84 and Sec5 to regulate the transport of membrane proteins in polarized epithelial cells, the translocation of GLUT4 to the plasma membrane, and mitochondrial fission during cell division. Clinical Significance Ral proteins, including RalA, have been associated with the progression of various cancers, such as bladder cancer and prostate cancer. Although the precise mechanisms remain unclear, studies suggest that RalA promotes anchorage-independent growth in cancer cells. Consequently, inhibition of RalA has been shown to suppress cancer initiation. Beyond its role in cancer, RalA's involvement in exocytosis in platelets, immune cells, neurons, and insulin regulation suggests that its dysregulation may contribute to pathological conditions such as thrombosis and metabolic syndrome. In patients with chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, Ral GTPases have been observed to exhibit heightened activity in platelets. Interactions RalA has been demonstrated to interact with several proteins, including: EXOC8 (Exocyst complex component 8), Filamin, PLD1 (Phospholipase D1), Sec5 (a component of the exocyst complex), RALBP1 (Ral-binding protein 1).
